record.context_brief: Erdos conjecture on divergent reciprocal sets
record.original_question: If A is a set of positive integers such that the reciprocal series sum_{n in A} 1/n diverges, must A contain arithmetic progressions of arbitrarily large finite length?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 1. (P. Erdős). If the sum of reciprocals of a set A of integers diverges, then that set contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions. This conjecture is still open even if one only seeks a single progression of length three.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ be a set of positive integers such that
$$\sum_{n \in A} \frac{1}{n} = \infty.$$
Prove or disprove: for every integer $k \geq 3$, the set $A$ contains a $k$-term arithmetic progression, i.e., there exist $a \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $d \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ such that $\{a, a+d, a+2d, \dots, a+(k-1)d\} \subseteq A$.
artifact.status_search_result: The full conjecture (for arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions) remains open. The case k=3 was resolved in 2020 by Bloom and Sisask, who proved that any set of positive integers with divergent reciprocal sum contains a 3-term arithmetic progression; quantitative improvements were made by Kelley–Meka (2023). The case k≥4 is still open.

status_evidence.title: Erdős conjecture on arithmetic progressions - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: The conjecture remains open. The k=3 case was proved by Bloom and Sisask in 2020.
status_evidence.claim: Conjecture is still open in general; k=3 case resolved by Bloom-Sisask.

status_evidence.title: Landmark Math Proof Clears Hurdle in Top Erdős Conjecture
status_evidence.snippet: Bloom and Sisask proved the conjecture for arithmetic progressions of length 3.
